## Agent Model

One of the core product decisions was that each agent profile should carry its own provider and model selection.

That means the system is not tied to a single workspace-wide model choice.

An agent profile includes:

`export const agentProfileSchema = z.object({

## Provider Abstraction

The provider layer uses a common adapter interface so the runtime does not care whether the backing model is:

That abstraction is the difference between a flexible orchestration platform and a model-specific app.

Featherless.ai was intentionally modeled as OpenAI-compatible instead of a custom provider branch. That avoids provider sprawl and keeps the system extensible.

## Runtime Design

The orchestration runtime has a small, explicit responsibility set:

The first important runtime guardrail is DAG validation: [...] For an MVP, DAG-only execution is the right constraint. Cycles, resumable long-running jobs, and schedulers all complicate failure handling and state recovery.

## Node Execution

`input`

`http_tool`
`output`

Each type maps to a different execution path:

`input`

That gives each node enough context to behave like a stage in a larger orchestration rather than a standalone chat call.

leads.title: Let’s Build a Self-Improving AI Agent That Learns From Your Feedback
leads.content:
The skill library tracks which skills were used in each trajectory. When feedback comes in, those skills get updated. If the feedback is positive (task success > 0.7), the skill’s success rate increases. If the feedback is negative, it decreases.

This creates a natural selection process. Good skills get used more because they have higher success rates. Bad skills get used less because they have lower success rates. Over time, the agent’s skill set evolves toward better approaches.

Users can also create new skills manually. If a response is particularly good, they can check a box and describe what made it good. That becomes a new skill that the agent can use in the future.

The feedback endpoint in the API handles this: [...] When a user asks a question, the agent retrieves relevant skills, enhances the query with skill context, and generates a response. That response is then evaluated, and if it’s good, the skills used get a boost.

This creates a positive feedback loop. Good skills get used more. Used skills get better. The agent improves over time.

Next, let’s see how the reinforcement learning system makes this improvement happen.

## Reinforcement Learning in Action

Reinforcement learning is what makes REFLEX self-improving. Every user interaction becomes a learning opportunity. Here’s how it works. [...] Combine RL with RAG, and you get something powerful: an agent that can both access knowledge and learn from experience. That’s what REFLEX does.

Here’s a simple example. A static agent might always use the same approach to answer questions. It doesn’t know if users prefer detailed explanations or quick summaries. It doesn’t learn that certain topics need web search while others can use the knowledge base.

REFLEX learns these patterns. It tracks which skills work best for which types of questions. It remembers what users rate highly. Over time, it gets better at matching the right approach to the right question.

leads.title: How are you handling long running AI agents without losing context or blowing up costs? : r/AI_Agents
leads.content:
The sweet spot we landed on separates task state from conversation memory completely: a small structured record of what's done, what's pending and the key results, which the agent reads to pick the next step instead of re-reading history. Raw tool output never goes in the window, it gets stored and referenced, and that is where most of the token blowup actually comes from. That same record is what makes it resumable, so a crash mid-task restarts from the last checkpoint instead of a bad mid-summary.

Image 19: u/HeyZaney avatar

HeyZaney

•2mo ago

For 4–5 calls I probably wouldn’t over-engineer it yet. The thing that made the biggest difference for us was separating session context from project state. [...] The agent’s context is disposable. It gets the specific piece of work it’s doing, the relevant decisions/requirements, blockers and whatever artefacts it needs. It can reason, use tools, make a mess of its context window, then disappear.

The durable bit lives outside the session: what’s been done, what’s currently being worked on, decisions that were made and why, blockers, dependencies, and what should happen next. The next agent/session queries that state rather than trying to reconstruct the project from the previous conversation. [...] I’d also be careful with summaries as the persistent layer. A summary of “what happened” and the actual current state of the work aren’t quite the same thing, especially once a human changes something between agent runs. I’d rather have one authoritative task/decision state and keep the history separately.

We actually ended up building this into WithNettle because we needed it while building another product with agents. Git still owns the code/technical docs; WithNettle is basically the shared work context that both we (humans) and the agents read/write through MCP.

So out of your four, I’d probably make #2 the foundation, use #1 for whatever the agent needs right now, make #4 query #2, and treat #3 more as history/checkpointing than the thing the next agent has to trust as truth.

leads.title: Self-hosted AI Agents | Adam Childs
leads.content:
- Greater Model Optionality - your own agent is highly configurable allowing selection of the right model for every operation: orchestration, delegation, or route-by-topic to meet your needs (Cost / Performance / Specialization / Privacy)
- Easier access to real-time information. Any real-time data-feed you have access to, is available. Current Cloud products offer some of this (and have easier access to data they own) but are limited in what they can call out to
- Freedom of query - less controls / safeguards. Note: you'll still be under T&C and safeguards of selected services and backbone models unless you are hosting your own [...] I gave a fun presentation on self-hosted open source agents last month to our local AI and Data Engineering group. My example setup was Hermes Agent (#1 on the openrouter app leader board).
Yes, there are significant security and data governance considerations to be aware of and handle! But someone is finding value in these setups! Openrouter is showing >36T tokens through Hermes Agent in the last 30 days, Mac minis have been difficult to get all year.
What is the value proposition of these self-hosted agents?
Here's what I found:
- Allows Security-capability trade-off: Greater Security Risk for Greater Capability. Grant all locally runnable tools and ability to install needed tools–> Greater functionality, Grant credentials for any MCP/API –> Greater data access [...] I asked Claude Code to say "ok." It cost me 28,500 tokens and $0.18.
The command was claude -p "Reply with exactly: ok" --output-format json. Four words in. One word back. The kind of reply that should cost nothing, or close enough to nothing that you'd never think to check.
The usage block tells the story. Input: 9,931. Cache write: 3,235. Cache read: 15,291. My four words were a rounding error. The rest is Claude Code loading its own furniture before it ever reads your prompt.
Here's the deal. Every single call bills your installed skills, your global CLAUDE.md, plugins, project session memory. All of it. Fresh input and cache write. Every time, whether that call touches any of it or not.

leads.title: Stop Fighting AI Agents and Build a Reusable Multi-Agent Dev Environment
leads.content:
### The Solution: Code Copilot Team

I open-sourced everything I learned into a single repo: Code Copilot Team - a set of reusable, opinionated templates and conventions for AI-assisted development with multi-agent delegation.

GitHub: 

It's built for Claude Code as the reference implementation, but the conventions port directly to Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Aider, and local LLMs.

### The Three-Phase Workflow

The core idea is simple: AI agents are powerful but they need structure. Not every task should be delegated, and delegation needs clear boundaries.

The workflow breaks every development cycle into three phases:

### Phase 1 — Plan [...] Adaptive configuration. Instead of manually choosing a template, the Agent Builder analyzes your project (stack, structure, dependencies, team size) and generates the most accurate copilot configuration for that specific context. A solo Python CLI tool doesn't need the same setup as a full-stack mono-repo with five contributors.
 Session monitoring and learning. With user permission, the Agent Builder observes copilot sessions: what rules get triggered, where the agent struggles, which patterns lead to rework; and refines the configuration automatically. Every session makes the next one better. This creates the kind of closed-loop that turns static rules into a living, self-improving system. [...] The foundation for this already exists in the repo's modular rule files and session-splitting conventions. The Agent Builder is the natural next step: moving from "here are good defaults" to "here's the optimal configuration for exactly what you're doing right now".

Also coming:

 More templates (mobile, data engineering, DevOps/IaC)
 Metrics tracking for token spend per phase
 CI integration patterns for agent-generated code
 Instructions for tags needed for WebMCP

The repo is MIT Licensed and actively maintained. If you're experimenting with AI-powered dev workflows, whether single-agent loops or multi-agent teams, I would love your feedback.

leads.title: Your First Multi-Agent Handoff Without Chaos
leads.content:
Put together:

run_id R-9912  
 handoff: router -> specialist_policy (H-2048)  
 tool: search_policy (840ms)  
 tool: fetch_doc (410ms)  
 specialist_result: "policy found, missing fare_type"  
 handoff: specialist_policy -> composer (H-2051)  
 output: clarifying_question  
 outcome: pending_user
Now you can debug. Now you can improve.

## A Real-World Failure Mode: The “Polite Loop”

Here’s a common one: agents keep handing off because nobody is allowed to decide.

   Specialist says: “Needs more info, ask user.”
   Composer says: “Let’s verify policy first.”
   Router sees uncertainty and routes again.
   Repeat.

The fix is a protocol rule:

## Decision ownership

   Router owns “what happens next”
   Specialist owns “what’s true”
   Composer owns “what’s said”

And a loop breaker: [...] ## The Three Building Blocks: Roles, Protocols, Logs

Think of multi-agent handoff design as a triangle:

1.   Roles define responsibilities.
2.   Protocols define what’s passed between roles.
3.   Logs define what you can debug and measure.

Get these right and the rest becomes tuning.

## Roles: Start With the Smallest Useful Division

You might be tempted to create five agents on day one. Don’t.

Your first multi-agent handoff should split along a natural seam:

   “Find info” vs “decide”
   “Plan” vs “execute”
   “Draft” vs “review”

A proven starter set:

## Agent 1: Router

   Classifies intent
   Selects which specialist(s) to involve
   Sets budgets and constraints

## Agent 2: Specialist [...] User  
 |  
 v  
Router Agent  
 - intent  
 - budgets  
 - pick specialist(s)  
 |  
 v  
Specialist Agent  
 - retrieve / compute  
 - cite evidence  
 - return structured findings  
 |  
 v  
Composer Agent  
 - decide what to say  
 - render answer  
 - ask 1 clarifying question if needed  
 |  
 v  
User
And the key: only the Router initiates handoffs.  
Specialists don’t spawn more agents. That’s how you prevent agent “family trees” and runaway cost.

## Logs: The Three Logs That Make Handoffs Debbugable

If you log one thing, log the handoff packet. If you log three, log these:

## 1) Handoff Log

Every handoff is a record:

   who → who
   why (intent + objective)
   what was passed (packet hash)
   timestamps (start/end)

This gives you a trace of delegation.

## 2) Tool Log

leads.title: I Let an AI Agent Handle a Multi-Step Task. Here's Where It Broke - DEV Community
leads.content:
Step 4 never happened. By the time I manually corrected Step 2 and regenerated Step 3, the agent had lost enough context that the email draft was generic and disconnected from the specific patterns we'd found.

The task wasn't impossible. The AI had all the capabilities needed. But the workflow broke because multi-step tasks require human-like judgment about when to branch, when to backtrack, and when to ask for clarification—and current AI agents don't handle these meta-decisions well.

## Where AI Agents Actually Break

After running dozens of similar experiments, I've identified the specific failure modes that plague multi-step AI workflows: [...] Ambiguity resolution fails silently. When an AI agent encounters ambiguity—multiple valid interpretations of a step—it doesn't stop to ask. It picks one interpretation (often the first or most common) and continues. By the time you realize it went the wrong direction, it's three steps downstream and the context is contaminated.

Context windows create artificial boundaries. Long multi-step workflows exceed token limits. The agent starts forgetting early decisions. Step 7 might contradict Step 2 because the original context has been truncated. Humans maintain a mental model of the entire task; agents lose coherence as context windows fill. [...] Progress isn't resumable. If a multi-step workflow breaks at Step 5 of 8, you can't just fix Step 5 and continue. The entire context is lost. You're starting from scratch. There's no equivalent of "pick up where we left off" in most agent frameworks.

## The Task Types That Work vs. Those That Don't

Through experimentation, I've developed a rough taxonomy of what current AI agents handle well versus where they consistently break:

Tasks that work:

 Linear workflows with no branching ("parse this, transform that, output result")
 Single-domain operations where context is narrow and well-defined
 Tasks where every step has exactly one correct next action
 Workflows where intermediate failures are obvious and early
 Short sequences (3-4 steps max) that fit comfortably in context windows

leads.title: Self-Hosted Pantheon vs Claude Managed Agents — A Real Cost Comparison - DEV Community
leads.content:
### What Self-Hosted Gives You

| Feature | Managed | Self-Hosted |
 --- 
| Custom orchestration logic | ❌ API-constrained | ✅ Full control |
| Filesystem access | ❌ Sandboxed | ✅ Native |
| Local tool execution | ❌ Limited | ✅ Full shell |
| Data leaves your machine | ✅ (it does) | ✅ Stays local |
| Custom inter-agent protocols | ❌ Anthropic's format | ✅ PAX or anything |
| Debugging visibility | ❌ Black box | ✅ Watch sessions live |
| Model mixing | ❌ Claude only | ✅ Any model |

## The Filesystem Problem [...] Pantheon (self-hosted): tmux-based persistent Claude Code sessions on local/VPS hardware. Custom orchestration via file-based coordination, PAX-format handoffs, and an Atlas orchestrator god session.

Both approaches run Claude models. The difference is who runs the infrastructure.

## Pricing at Scale

### Managed Agents

### Pantheon (self-hosted)

Verdict: Self-hosted saves 60–70% at moderate scale. Managed Agents pricing inverts once you hit 4+ persistent agents.

## Control Tradeoffs

### What Managed Agents Give You [...] ## The Real Question

The managed vs. self-hosted debate isn't about technology. It's about what you're building.

If agents are a feature you're selling → Managed makes sense.  
  
If agents are your production infrastructure → Self-hosted wins.

Pantheon is production infrastructure. Every god session has real filesystem access, runs real deployments, and coordinates through real files. No amount of hosted convenience is worth losing that.

But for teams building the next Whoff Agents — selling agent capabilities to others — Managed Agents at $0.08/session-hour is a reasonable starting point. Just model your pricing before you scale.

leads.title: Claude Managed Agents: What It Actually Offers, the Honest Pros and Cons, and How to Run Agents Yourself | by unicodeveloper | Medium
leads.content:
Self-host if:

 You need model flexibility (mixing Claude, GPT-5, open-source models for different tasks)
 Data privacy requirements mean agent workloads can’t leave your infrastructure
 You’re running high-volume workloads where $0.08/session-hour adds up
 You need features in “research preview” to be stable and available now
 You already have engineering capacity to own the infrastructure layer
 You’re in a regulated industry with strict data residency requirements

Consider Multica if: You want the team/task management UX (agents as colleagues, skill sharing, Kanban) with multi-model flexibility and self-hosting. [...] ## Get unicodeveloper’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Model compatibility: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, OpenClaw, OpenCode. Vendor-neutral by design.

Where it falls short vs. Claude Managed Agents: No container-level sandboxing with credential vault isolation. No tool-call tracing at the level Claude Console provides. It’s an orchestration and task management layer on top of existing CLIs, not a compute execution infrastructure. If you need deep security isolation (credential vaults, scoped network access per agent run), Multica doesn’t provide that out of the box.

Where it wins: Multi-model, fully self-hostable, richer team collaboration UX (Kanban boards, agent profiles, skill sharing), and zero vendor dependency. Free to self-host. [...] Anthropic’s enterprise tier has data privacy commitments, but that’s a different question from whether you want your most sensitive operational data flowing through a third-party cloud at all. The developer community has been vocal about this: “security nightmare” comes up frequently when agents have access to real systems.

### Pricing at scale needs modeling

$0.08 per session-hour sounds cheap. For a fleet of agents processing long tasks, model the numbers before you commit. A 24-agent system each running 8-hour daily tasks is $15.36/day in session overhead, before inference costs. At some point, you might have to ask yourself if its cheaper to just have an engineer handle it especially if you’re not making the kind of money from customers that offsets the cost.

leads.title:
Cursor Self-Hosted Machines draws its security boundary through the middle of one agent session.

The commands move to your network. The model and planning remain in Cursor’s cloud.

That split can… | Omid Saffari
leads.content:
But the loop cannot plan blind. Selected file contents, terminal output, diffs, screenshots, local MCP results, and routing metadata still go back to Cursor. Privacy Mode keeps that code out of training. It does not make the session offline.
This lets a security team approve two separate things: where tools execute, and where the context used by the model is processed. Calling the whole setup “self-hosted” and stopping the review there misses the second half.
The same split applies to cost. Managed Cloud Agents include the execution machine. Self-hosted agents keep Cursor’s model charges, require an Enterprise contract for Team Pools, and add the worker bill plus base-image maintenance, isolation, patching, cleanup, and capacity. [...] Cursor’s Cloudflare template makes that visible. The smallest reference shape is 0.5 vCPU, 4 GiB of memory, and 8 GB of disk. Under one specific model of 100 one-hour sessions plus a five-minute idle window, the container line comes to about $11.993 for the month after included usage.
That figure excludes the Enterprise contract, model use, Worker and Durable Object usage, logs, egress, R2, and the people maintaining it.
Self-host when private tools, custom hardware, or a custom image justify owning the worker. If managed networking already reaches what the agent needs, the extra fleet buys no new model capability.
Approve the execution boundary and the context boundary separately, then price both. [...] 5. End at a pull request with test evidence. Keep CI, human review, staging, and release unchanged.
That turns the agent into an asynchronous implementation lane, not an unsupervised owner of production.
The business math then gets simple. Take a 40-hour task at an illustrative $100 an hour. Human-led implementation costs $4,000.
If the agent-led lane needs four 30-minute checkpoints and 3 hours of final review, the team spends 5 human hours, or $500. That leaves a maximum of $3,500 for model and tool costs before the labor advantage disappears.
It is not a promised $3,500 saving. If the pull request needs another 35 human hours of correction, the advantage is gone before the model bill even matters.

leads.title: Multi-Agent Coordination: Message-Bus Patterns That Keep Agents Sane - DEV Community
leads.content:
A handoff transfers control. Agent A finishes, hands the whole conversation to Agent B, and steps out. This reads well in a demo. In production it means the transcript grows on every hop, and by the fourth agent you are paying to re-read a conversation nobody trimmed. Handoffs also lose the parent: once A hands off to B, nobody is holding the original task to check the final answer against it.

A shared bus keeps a supervisor in charge. Workers never talk to each other. They receive a small typed task, do the work, and return a small typed artifact to the supervisor, which composes the result. This is the shape of Anthropic's research system, and it is the default you should reach for. [...] The test is one question: does a worker need to see what a sibling just produced? If yes, you do not have parallel workers. You have a sequential pipeline pretending to be a team, and you should run it as one ordered chain, not as free-form handoffs.

Here is the bus shape in the bare Anthropic SDK. Three workers fan out, the supervisor merges. No worker touches another worker. [...] `await`

## The one rule to keep

If a worker needs to see what a sibling produced, you do not have a parallel team. Keep workers isolated, hand them small typed tasks, make them return small typed artifacts, and put the budget in the envelope. Do that and the supervisor-worker shape stays cheap, traceable, and debuggable. Skip it and the same pattern turns into a group chat that argues with itself until the bill arrives.

— Create custom subagents

Claude Code provides several built-in subagents: explore, plan, general purpose, status line, and Claude Code guidelines. You can read more about each of them in the documentation.

However, and this is where it gets interesting, you can define a specialized subagent through a dedicated Markdown file with a specific front matter in a `.claude/agents` folder. The front matter defines: a name, a description, a model, and a list of available tools. The body describes the subagent's purpose, i.e., its instructions. Here's a sample:

`.claude/agents`
`---
name: code-reviewer
description: "Reviews code for quality and best practices"
tools: Read, Glob, Grep
model: sonnet [...] Claude Code's experimental Agent Teams feature is an early implementation: multiple instances work in parallel on a shared codebase, where teammates operate in their own context windows and communicate directly with each other. Anthropic used 16 parallel agents to build a C compiler from scratch that can compile Linux. Cursor ran hundreds of concurrent agents for weeks to build a web browser from scratch and migrate their own codebase from Solid to React.

Obviously, I have neither the resources nor the know-how to tackle such a huge undertaking. However, I wanted to design a team to handle smaller tasks.

Your agent answered a question, perfectly last Tuesday. Ask the same question today. It has no idea what you are talking about.

## Best suited for

Self-hosted deployment earns its operational burden in two scenarios: when compliance makes it non-negotiable, and when volume makes cloud inference economics unsustainable. Often these arrive together — regulated industries with high-frequency workloads, where keeping data on-premises and controlling inference cost are both requirements rather than preferences. The team capability to run this stack isn’t optional; it’s a prerequisite for the choice to hold.

## Option 3: Hybrid Deployment

Hybrid deployment splits your agent’s workload deliberately across cloud and local infrastructure, based on the nature of each task and the data involved. A self-hosted orchestration and routing layer sits in the middle, deciding where each request goes. [...] That’s where the easy part ends.

Deploying an AI agent to production isn’t like deploying a REST API or a microservice. Agents maintain state, execute multi-step workflows, invoke external tools, and often process sensitive data. The infrastructure decisions you make at this stage shape everything that follows — cost, latency, security, compliance, and how easily the system scales months or years later.

In practice, most production deployments fall into one of three architectures: cloud, self-hosted (local), or hybrid. None is universally better for every workload. Each optimizes for a different set of constraints. This article will help you understand those trade-offs so you can choose the architecture that best fits your workload.

## Why Agent Deployment Is Different [...] ## Best suited for

Cloud is the right default for teams that haven’t built ML infrastructure and aren’t planning to — where the priority is getting something into production quickly, the data involved isn’t regulated or confidential, and traffic is unpredictable enough that elastic scaling is a genuine advantage rather than a marketing feature. If none of your constraints push you toward local, start here.

## Option 2: Self-Hosted (Local) Deployment

Self-Hosted (Local) deployment means everything runs on infrastructure you own and operate. The model weights live on your machines, the agent runtime runs on your servers, and nothing leaves your network unless you decide it should.

leads.title: AI Agent Design Patterns Playlist — Part 4: Multi-Agent Patterns
leads.content:
User request  
 ↓  
Router  
 ├── Data agent → SQL, dashboards, metrics  
 ├── Policy agent → approved knowledge base  
 └── Support agent → CRM and ticketing system
The router does not need database access. The policy agent does not need permission to modify a customer ticket. Splitting the system lets you apply the least-privilege principle and test each capability independently.

> _Rule of thumb:__add another agent only when it has a distinct role, toolset, permission boundary, or evaluation method._

## 1. Router and handoff pattern

The router classifies the request and forwards it to the most appropriate specialist.

“Why was my invoice rejected?”  
 ↓  
 Router  
 ↓  
 Billing specialist  
 ↓  
Answer based on billing records and policy
## Router responsibilities [...] Identify the request’s domain or intent.
   Select a specialist, deterministic workflow, or human queue.
   Pass only the context needed by the selected destination.
   Handle low-confidence cases safely.

## Handoff responsibilities

A handoff should preserve the conversation’s important context:

   the user’s original request;
   relevant facts already collected;
   constraints and requested output format;
   a reason for the handoff;
   what has already been attempted.

Avoid handing the entire transcript to every agent by default. A concise, structured handoff is cheaper, more private, and less likely to confuse the recipient.

## Example routing policy [...] Use schemas, append-only evidence logs, versioning, and conflict rules when several agents write to the same state.

## A runnable Python example: router, specialists, and a supervisor

This example uses simple deterministic rules rather than an LLM. It demonstrates the architecture: a router chooses a specialist, each specialist returns structured evidence, and a supervisor formats the answer.

drafts.text: The per-profile provider/model choice is the right call. In practice, the tricky part is keeping orchestration state separate from model config so swapping a worker from Ollama to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint doesn't break the graph. How are you handling per-agent context windows and token budgets when mixing local and remote models? Disclosure: I work on AutoByteus, and we hit similar friction around evaluation when agents use different providers.

“When feedback comes in, those skills get updated” is a useful starting point, but I’d be careful about updating every skill in a trajectory from one outcome. A successful response can still contain weak steps, and a failed one can include useful skills. Attributing feedback at the step or skill level, with confidence and rollback, makes the loop safer. Disclosure: I work on AutoByteus, where evaluation-driven feedback informs future tasks.

Separating task state from conversation memory is the cleanest way to handle this. Keeping raw tool outputs out of the window is essential for cost control. Disclosure: I work on AutoByteus, where we use that structured record to let specialist agents hand off work. It also helps to store feedback from failures as reusable skills, so the next session starts with better instructions rather than just a summary of what happened.

Selection of the right model for every operation" is the key insight. The harder problem is knowing which model actually works best for each operation. Without evaluation, you're guessing based on benchmarks that may not reflect your tasks. Disclosure: I work on AutoByteus, and we've found that capturing feedback from specialist agent outputs is what turns configurability into actual improvement over time.

The "reusable, opinionated templates and conventions" framing is the right abstraction — most teams rebuild this scaffolding per project. One thing worth exploring: making the conventions themselves evolvable, so session feedback refines the templates rather than just the config. Disclosure: I work on AutoByteus, where agent feedback becomes reusable skills for the next task. Curious how your Agent Builder decides which patterns are worth codifying versus discarding.
